walkthroughs.body_html: Park (1991) proposed a 3-phase model. Quality of life axis (y) vs time (x). Sharp drop at impact; gradual recovery thereafter. Curve can return below, to, or above pre-event level. Steepness of recovery reflects governance capacity and external aid.

Mw 9.0 + tsunami killed 18500; displaced 470000. JSDF mobilised 100000 personnel within 24 hours. Reconstruction budget ~£200 billion. Coastal sea walls rebuilt to 15 m. By 2021 most areas above pre-event quality of life via build-back-better policy.

Mw 7.8 (April) killed 9000; damaged 800000 homes. Six months later 70 percent still in temporary shelter; political deadlock delayed funds. By 2023 only 75 percent of homes rebuilt; many to original standards. Highlights how governance constrains Park's curve.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a natural hazard and a natural disaster?
options: A hazard happens on land and a disaster happens at sea.
Climate change only happens in summer.
A natural hazard is a physical event with potential to cause harm; it becomes a disaster only when it affects vulnerable people and causes significant impact.
They are the same thing — any earthquake or hurricane is a disaster.

mcqs.q: Why do earthquakes of similar magnitude cause different amounts of damage?
options: A hazard happens on land and a disaster happens at sea.
Damage depends on depth, distance from population, building quality, ground type (liquefaction risk), time of day, and emergency preparedness — not just magnitude.
All earthquakes of magnitude 7 cause the same damage everywhere.
Bigger magnitude always means more deaths.

mcqs.q: Why can a cold winter NOT disprove climate change?
options: All earthquakes of magnitude 7 cause the same damage everywhere.
Climate change only happens in summer.
Climate is the long-term statistical average; a single cold winter is a weather event. Climate change is the trend in averages and extremes over decades, not the absence of cold days.
A really cold winter proves global warming is not happening.
